_meta.description: Authored teaching primers keyed by primary tag. scripts/gen-paths.js looks up each chapter's primary tag here; if matched, the chapter's concept node gets these flashcards instead of auto-derived ones. Fallback (truncation-fixed) is still used for unmatched tags.

security.title: Security fundamentals
security.intro: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

networking.title: Networking fundamentals
networking.intro: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

storage.title: Storage concepts
storage.intro: Cloud storage comes in three flavors with very different cost/perf trade-offs: object (think S3), block (think EBS / managed disks), and file (think EFS / Azure Files / Filestore). Pick wrong and you either overpay or hit performance ceilings.

flashcards.front: Object vs block vs file storage — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Object (S3, Blob, GCS) for unstructured data, backups, static sites, data lakes — flat namespace, HTTP API, infinite scale. Block (EBS, managed disks) for OS disks and databases — low latency, single attach. File (EFS, NFS) when multiple VMs need a shared POSIX filesystem.

flashcards.front: What is a storage class / tier?
flashcards.back: Same data, different SLA and price. Hot tier (frequent access, expensive read, cheap retrieval). Cold/archive tier (rare access, cheap to store, expensive to read, retrieval latency from minutes to hours). Lifecycle policies move data between tiers automatically.

flashcards.front: Why use server-side encryption?
flashcards.back: Data is encrypted at rest by the storage service using either provider-managed keys (default, no extra config) or your own keys via KMS. This protects against physical disk theft and meets compliance baselines without changing your app code.

flashcards.front: What's storage durability vs availability?
flashcards.back: Durability is the chance your data won't be lost (object stores claim ~11 9s — 99.999999999%). Availability is the chance you can reach it right now (typically 4 9s — 99.99%). Durability is multi-region replication; availability is how many concurrent failures the service tolerates.

compute.title: Compute services
compute.intro: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

flashcards.front: What is autoscaling?
flashcards.back: A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.

flashcards.front: Reserved / committed-use vs on-demand pricing.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

iam.title: Identity and access management
iam.intro: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

flashcards.front: Identity-based vs resource-based policies.
flashcards.back: Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

flashcards.front: Why federation / SSO?
flashcards.back: Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

monitoring.title: Observability and monitoring
monitoring.intro: Observability is metrics + logs + traces — the three pillars. You need all three to debug a production incident: metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where in the call graph the problem lives.

flashcards.front: Metrics vs logs vs traces — what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Metrics: numeric time-series, cheap to store, perfect for dashboards and alerts ('p99 latency = 800 ms'). Logs: discrete events with context, expensive at scale, perfect for forensics. Traces: causally-linked spans showing a request's full path through services.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an alert and a notification?
flashcards.back: An alert is a condition that fires when a metric crosses a threshold (CPU > 80% for 5 min). The notification is the resulting message (email, Slack, PagerDuty page). One alert can fan out to many notifications. Tuning alerts is harder than wiring notifications.

flashcards.front: What is an SLI / SLO / SLA?
flashcards.back: SLI (indicator): the metric you actually measure ('% of requests under 200 ms'). SLO (objective): the internal target ('99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 28 days'). SLA (agreement): the contractual promise to customers, usually weaker than the SLO so you have buffer.

flashcards.front: Why structured logs?
flashcards.back: Plain-text logs are unparseable at scale. Structured logs (JSON, with timestamp + level + service + request_id + key fields) are indexable, queryable, and join-able across services. Most platforms auto-extract fields from JSON without configuration.

vpn.title: VPN and secure connectivity
vpn.intro: A VPN tunnels private traffic over the public internet, encrypting it end-to-end. Site-to-site VPNs connect networks (e.g., on-prem to cloud); client VPNs connect individual devices to a private network. Both rely on IPsec or SSL/TLS.

flashcards.front: Site-to-site VPN vs client VPN — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Site-to-site VPN connects two networks (typical: on-prem data center ↔ cloud VPC) using gateway devices on each side. Client VPN connects an individual user's laptop to a private network for remote access. Site-to-site uses IPsec, client VPN often uses SSL or WireGuard.

flashcards.front: IPsec — IKE phase 1 vs phase 2.
flashcards.back: Phase 1 (IKE) authenticates the two peers (pre-shared key or certificate) and builds a secure management channel. Phase 2 negotiates the actual data tunnel (encryption algorithm, key lifetime). Most exam questions test that phase 1 must succeed before phase 2.

flashcards.front: When do you pick a dedicated link over a VPN?
flashcards.back: VPN over the public internet is cheap but variable — bandwidth and latency depend on internet weather. Dedicated links (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute, Cloud Interconnect) are private fiber with consistent latency and bandwidth — pick them for production traffic that must be predictable, or compliance scenarios that forbid the public internet.

flashcards.front: What's the BGP tunnel option for?
flashcards.back: VPNs can use static routes or BGP. BGP-based VPNs auto-propagate route changes between sides (add a new subnet on-prem → cloud learns it within seconds). Static VPN requires manual route updates every time the topology changes. Always pick BGP for production.

routing.title: IP routing
routing.intro: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.front: What's the longest-prefix-match rule?
flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

flashcards.front: Default route — what does `0.0.0.0/0` mean?
flashcards.back: It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

flashcards.front: Administrative distance — what is it?
flashcards.back: When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

ospf.title: OSPF
ospf.intro: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state interior gateway protocol — every router floods its neighbors with link-state advertisements (LSAs), builds an identical map of the network, and runs Dijkstra to find shortest paths.

flashcards.front: What is an OSPF area, and why use multiple?
flashcards.back: An area is a group of OSPF routers that share full link-state info. ABRs (area border routers) summarize between areas. Single-area is fine for small networks (~50 routers); multi-area limits LSA flooding scope and reduces SPF computation as the network grows.

flashcards.front: What is area 0?
flashcards.back: The backbone area. All non-zero areas MUST connect to area 0, directly or via a virtual link. Inter-area traffic always passes through area 0. If area 0 partitions, OSPF breaks.

flashcards.front: Cost calculation — what's the formula?
flashcards.back: Default cost = reference-bandwidth ÷ interface-bandwidth. Reference defaults to 100 Mbps, so a 100 Mbps link costs 1, a 10 Mbps link costs 10. On modern networks you should raise the reference (e.g., to 1000) so 1G+ links get distinguishable costs.

flashcards.front: DR / BDR — what problem do they solve?
flashcards.back: On a multi-access segment (Ethernet), if every router formed a full adjacency with every other, you'd get O(n²) flooding. OSPF elects a Designated Router (DR) and Backup DR. Other routers only fully adjacency with the DR/BDR; the DR re-floods. The election uses priority then router ID.

bgp.title: BGP
bgp.intro: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol of the internet. It runs between autonomous systems (ASes) and is a path-vector protocol — instead of a metric, each route carries the full list of ASes it has traversed.

flashcards.front: eBGP vs iBGP — what's different?
flashcards.back: eBGP runs between routers in different ASes; it's how the internet is glued together. iBGP runs between routers inside the same AS — it carries external routes to internal routers. iBGP requires a full mesh (or route reflectors) because routes learned via iBGP are NOT re-advertised to other iBGP peers.

flashcards.front: What is AS_PATH and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: AS_PATH is the list of autonomous systems a route has traversed, prepended at each AS boundary. It's the primary loop-prevention mechanism (a router rejects a route already containing its own AS) and the second tie-breaker in BGP best-path selection — shorter path wins.

flashcards.front: BGP best-path attributes — name the top three.
flashcards.back: (1) Highest LOCAL_PREF wins (locally configured 'prefer this exit'). (2) Shortest AS_PATH. (3) Lowest ORIGIN code (IGP < EGP < incomplete). Then MED, then eBGP > iBGP, then lowest IGP cost, then router-ID tie-breaker. LOCAL_PREF is how you steer outbound; AS_PATH prepending is how you influence inbound.

flashcards.front: Why does BGP need a route reflector?
flashcards.back: iBGP requires a full mesh (every router peers with every other) — O(n²) sessions, doesn't scale. A route reflector breaks the rule: it re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients. Clients only peer with the RR. One RR + 100 clients = 100 sessions vs. 5,000 for a full mesh.

stp.title: Spanning Tree Protocol
stp.intro: STP prevents loops on Ethernet networks by blocking redundant links. Without it, a single redundant cable between two switches creates a broadcast storm that takes the LAN down. STP automatically picks one root bridge and computes a loop-free tree.

flashcards.front: Why is loop prevention needed on Ethernet?
flashcards.back: Ethernet frames have no TTL — once a broadcast frame enters a loop it circulates forever, doubling on every pass, until the LAN melts. STP detects redundant paths and blocks them, leaving a spanning tree. If the active link fails, STP unblocks an alternate.

flashcards.front: How is the root bridge elected?
flashcards.back: Lowest bridge ID wins. Bridge ID = priority (default 32768, lower is better) followed by MAC address. In practice you set the priority on your core switches so root election is predictable, not whoever happens to have the lowest MAC.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between RSTP and classic STP?
flashcards.back: Classic 802.1D converges in 30-50 seconds (listen → learn → forward). RSTP (802.1w) converges in 1-2 seconds by negotiating port roles between adjacent switches instead of timing them out. Always use RSTP — classic STP is too slow for modern data centers.

flashcards.front: Portfast / Bridge Assurance — when do you enable them?
flashcards.back: PortFast bypasses the listening/learning states on access ports (anywhere an end host plugs in) — link comes up forwarding immediately. NEVER enable PortFast on a switch-to-switch trunk; it lets loops form during reconvergence.

vlan.title: VLANs
vlan.intro: A VLAN logically segments a single physical switch into multiple broadcast domains. VLAN 10 traffic can't see VLAN 20 traffic without a Layer-3 routed hop, even on the same switch. This is the foundation of multi-tenant networking on shared hardware.

flashcards.front: Access port vs trunk port — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN and strips the tag — end hosts don't see VLAN headers. A trunk port carries multiple VLANs between switches using 802.1Q tags. Hosts plug into access ports; switches connect to each other via trunks.

flashcards.front: What is the native VLAN on a trunk?
flashcards.back: The native VLAN is the one VLAN that's NOT tagged on a trunk — frames in that VLAN traverse the link with no 802.1Q header. Defaults to VLAN 1 but should be changed to an unused VLAN on every trunk for security (prevents VLAN hopping attacks).

flashcards.front: Why use a Layer-3 SVI?
flashcards.back: A Switched Virtual Interface (SVI) gives a VLAN a Layer-3 address inside the switch — it's the inter-VLAN router. Without an SVI (or external router), VLANs can't talk to each other. Modern switches do inter-VLAN routing in hardware at wire speed.

flashcards.front: What's VLAN hopping?
flashcards.back: An attacker tricks the switch into forwarding their traffic into a VLAN they shouldn't be in. Two flavors: double-tagging (exploits the native-VLAN-untagged rule) and switch-spoofing (the host negotiates a trunk via DTP). Mitigation: tag the native VLAN, set ports to access mode explicitly, disable DTP.

s3.title: Amazon S3
s3.intro: S3 is AWS's object store — flat namespace of buckets containing objects, accessed via HTTP. It backs almost every AWS architecture: data lakes, static sites, backups, lambda triggers, CloudFront origins. The exam tests storage classes, encryption, access control, and event notifications.

flashcards.front: S3 storage classes — pick one for backups, one for hot data, one for archive.
flashcards.back: Hot: S3 Standard (high cost, instant access). Backups / infrequent: S3 Standard-IA (cheaper storage, retrieval fee). Archive: Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest storage, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle policies move objects between classes automatically based on age.

flashcards.front: S3 bucket policy vs IAM policy vs ACL — which to use?
flashcards.back: IAM policy: 'this user/role can read bucket X'. Bucket policy: 'these principals can access this bucket' — required for cross-account and public access. ACL (legacy): per-object permissions, mostly avoided today. Use bucket policies for most cross-account, IAM for in-account.

flashcards.front: How do you make an S3 website (static-site hosting)?
flashcards.back: Enable static-website hosting on the bucket, upload index.html, set a bucket policy allowing public-read on objects, point a CloudFront distribution at it for HTTPS + edge caching. Don't expose the bucket directly — CloudFront with an OAC (Origin Access Control) is the canonical pattern.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between server-side and client-side encryption?
flashcards.back: SSE: data encrypted by S3 after upload. Variants: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed key, easiest), SSE-KMS (your KMS key, audit trail), SSE-C (you supply the key on each request). Client-side: you encrypt before upload — S3 only sees ciphertext. Pick SSE-KMS for compliance, SSE-S3 for default-on.

lambda.title: AWS Lambda
lambda.intro: Lambda runs your code in response to events (API call, S3 upload, EventBridge schedule, SQS message). No servers to manage. You pay for invocations and execution time. The exam tests limits, cold starts, triggers, and the IAM execution role.

flashcards.front: Lambda execution limits — memory, time, payload?
flashcards.back: Memory: 128 MB - 10 GB (CPU scales with memory). Timeout: max 15 minutes. Sync invocation payload: 6 MB. Async invocation payload: 256 KB. Deployment package (zipped): 50 MB direct upload, 250 MB via S3, 10 GB via container image.

flashcards.front: Cold start — what is it and how do you minimize it?
flashcards.back: First invocation of an idle function takes 100 ms - 2 s extra to load the runtime and your code. Mitigations: provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed instances), smaller deployment packages, native-compiled runtimes (Go, Rust), keeping connections out of the handler so they're reused across invocations.

flashcards.front: Sync vs async vs poll-based invocation.
flashcards.back: Sync (API Gateway, ALB): caller waits for result. Async (S3, SNS, EventBridge): Lambda queues and retries on failure. Poll-based (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams): Lambda pulls records, processes in batches, manages retries via the source. Each has different retry semantics — read the docs.

flashcards.front: How does Lambda get permissions to call other AWS services?
flashcards.back: Each function has an IAM execution role. The role's policies say what the function CAN do (read S3, write DynamoDB, decrypt KMS). Lambda assumes the role on every invocation and exposes temporary credentials to your code via the SDK.

vpc.title: Amazon VPC
vpc.intro: A VPC is a logically isolated network inside an AWS region. You define the IP range, create subnets in multiple AZs, route tables decide where packets go, and security groups + NACLs filter what's allowed. Most networking exam Qs are VPC-shaped.

flashcards.front: Public vs private subnet — what makes the difference?
flashcards.back: Routing. A 'public' subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway (0.0.0.0/0 → IGW). A 'private' subnet doesn't — its instances can reach the internet only via a NAT Gateway (outbound) or VPC endpoint (to specific AWS services). The subnet's CIDR doesn't determine its category — the route table does.

flashcards.front: Security group vs network ACL — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Security group: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), applied per ENI / instance, default deny, allow rules only. NACL: stateless (must allow return traffic explicitly), applied per subnet, supports allow and deny rules, evaluated in numbered order. SGs handle 95% of cases; NACLs add a deny-list at the subnet edge.

flashcards.front: What's a NAT Gateway for?
flashcards.back: Lets instances in a private subnet initiate outbound internet traffic (package updates, API calls to public endpoints) while remaining unreachable from the internet. The NAT replaces the source IP with its own elastic IP. One per AZ for HA — they're zonal, not regional.

flashcards.front: VPC peering vs Transit Gateway — when to scale up?
flashcards.back: Peering connects two VPCs (mesh: N VPCs need N×(N-1)/2 peerings). It's free per-GB but doesn't transit. Transit Gateway is a hub: many VPCs and on-prem VPNs all connect to it, full transitive routing. Use peering up to ~5 VPCs; switch to TGW when the mesh becomes painful.

cryptography.title: Cryptography fundamentals
cryptography.intro: Crypto is the math layer that makes the rest of security possible. Most exam questions test symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing vs encryption, when to use which, and how key management actually works in practice.

flashcards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Symmetric (AES-256, ChaCha20): one shared key, fast, used for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): public/private key pair, slow, used to exchange a symmetric key or to sign. Real systems use both: asymmetric to negotiate, symmetric to encrypt the bulk traffic (this is how TLS works).

flashcards.front: What's the difference between hashing and encryption?
flashcards.back: Encryption is reversible — the holder of the key can recover the plaintext. Hashing is one-way — you cannot derive the input from the output. Hashes are for integrity (did the file change?) and password storage (compare hashes, never store plaintext). SHA-256 is the modern default; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken.

flashcards.front: What is a digital signature?
flashcards.back: A signature is a hash of the message encrypted with the signer's private key. Anyone with the public key can verify (decrypt the signature, recompute the hash, check they match). This proves authenticity (the holder of the private key signed it) AND integrity (the message wasn't tampered with).

flashcards.front: Why use a key management service (KMS)?
flashcards.back: Raw key handling is hard to do safely — you have to rotate, audit, restrict, destroy. A KMS holds keys in hardware, exposes encrypt/decrypt APIs, logs every use, enforces who can use which key. Your application code never sees the actual key material. AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS all play this role.

governance.title: Cloud governance
governance.intro: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

flashcards.front: What is a landing zone?
flashcards.back: A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

billing.title: Cloud billing and cost
billing.intro: Cloud cost optimization is mostly visibility + commitments. You can't optimize what you can't see, and you can't commit without forecasts. Most exams test the savings instruments (reserved instances, savings plans, sustained use) and the visibility tools.

flashcards.front: Where do you see cloud spend?
flashcards.back: AWS Cost Explorer / Azure Cost Management / GCP Billing reports. Filter by tag, service, account, region. Set up budget alerts (notify when 80% / 100% of monthly budget is hit) so a runaway autoscaler doesn't surprise you on the 28th.

flashcards.front: Reserved Instance vs Savings Plan vs Spot — pick the right one.
flashcards.back: RI / committed-use: 1-3 yr commitment, 30-60% off, locked to instance family/region. Savings Plan: 1-3 yr commitment on $/hr spend, more flexible across instance types. Spot/preemptible: up to 90% off, can be reclaimed any moment. Use commitments for steady baseline, spot for fault-tolerant workloads.

flashcards.front: What's the egress (data transfer out) cost trap?
flashcards.back: Most clouds charge nothing to ingest data but $0.05-$0.12/GB to send it OUT. Inter-region replication, public-facing APIs, multi-cloud data movement — all add up fast. Mitigations: same-region peering, CloudFront / CDN caching, VPC endpoints to keep traffic on the AWS backbone.

flashcards.front: What is a unit cost / cost per X?
flashcards.back: Cost-per-request, cost-per-active-user, cost-per-transaction. Total cloud spend is a vanity metric — engineers can't act on '$50k/month'. Unit cost ($0.003 per request) reveals whether you got cheaper or more expensive as you scaled, which is what optimization actually means.

automation.title: Automation and IaC
automation.intro: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining your servers, networks, databases in version-controlled config files instead of clicking around a console. Pipelines automate the apply step. The combination is what makes cloud reproducible.

flashcards.front: What is the value of declarative IaC?
flashcards.back: You describe the desired state ('I want 3 EC2 instances in this VPC'), the tool figures out how to get there. Reruns are idempotent — applying the same code twice doesn't double anything. State drift (someone clicked in the console) is detected on the next plan/diff.

flashcards.front: Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Bicep — what's different?
flashcards.back: Terraform: cloud-agnostic, HCL syntax, plan/apply workflow, huge ecosystem. CloudFormation: AWS-only, YAML/JSON, native rollback. Bicep: Azure-only, cleaner DSL on top of ARM. Pick the cloud-native tool if you're single-cloud; Terraform if multi-cloud or your team prefers HCL.

flashcards.front: What is a CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure?
flashcards.back: Same as for app code: commit → run linter (tflint) → plan / diff → require approval → apply. Production typically has a manual approval gate; lower environments auto-apply. Plan output is reviewed in the PR so a destructive change is caught before merge.

flashcards.front: Why is mutable infrastructure considered an anti-pattern?
flashcards.back: Mutable: SSH in, run apt-get, edit configs, server drifts from its template. Two 'identical' servers slowly diverge → snowflakes → 'works on this instance only' bugs. Immutable: bake a fresh AMI / image, replace the running instance, the old one is destroyed. Painful upfront, trivial to roll back, no drift.

cli.title: Command-line tooling
cli.intro: Most exam workflows involve `aws`, `az`, `gcloud`, or `kubectl`. Knowing the structure of each (resource → command → flags) saves you in the lab portion and in real life. They're all roughly the same shape with different naming conventions.

flashcards.front: How do you authenticate the AWS CLI?
flashcards.back: `aws configure` writes credentials to `~/.aws/credentials` (access key + secret) and `~/.aws/config` (region, output format). Use named profiles for multi-account: `aws s3 ls --profile prod`. Prefer `aws configure sso` or temporary STS credentials over long-lived access keys.

flashcards.front: What does `kubectl get` do, and what flags are essential?
flashcards.back: Lists resources of a kind: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl get nodes`. Key flags: `-n <namespace>` (default is `default`), `-o wide` (more columns), `-o yaml` (full manifest), `--watch` (live updates), `-l label=value` (filter by label).

flashcards.front: Output formatting — JSON, table, text?
flashcards.back: AWS / Azure / gcloud all support `--output json|text|table|yaml`. JSON is for piping into `jq` for scripts. Table is for humans browsing in the terminal. Always set a default in your config so you don't squint at JSON when browsing.

flashcards.front: How do you find a command's options without leaving the terminal?
flashcards.back: `aws <service> <command> help` (or `--help`), `kubectl <verb> --help`, `az <group> <command> --help`. These open built-in docs with every flag listed. Searching the official web docs is for concepts; for syntax, the local help is always current.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting methodology
troubleshooting.intro: A structured troubleshooting process beats random guessing every time. The classic flow: identify the problem precisely, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. Most exams test that you know the flow AND can spot the layer at which the symptom originates.

flashcards.front: What's the standard troubleshooting model?
flashcards.back: CompTIA's 6-step: (1) Identify the problem (gather symptoms, questions to user, recent changes). (2) Establish a theory of probable cause. (3) Test the theory. (4) Plan and implement the fix. (5) Verify full system functionality, apply preventive measures. (6) Document everything.

flashcards.front: Top-down vs bottom-up troubleshooting on a network problem.
flashcards.back: Top-down: start at the application layer and work down — does the browser work? DNS? TCP? Routing? Bottom-up: start at the physical layer — is the cable plugged in? Link light? IP? When you suspect physical/cable, bottom-up is faster. When the user has 'a website is broken', top-down is faster.

flashcards.front: Why ask 'what changed recently'?
flashcards.back: Almost every production incident traces back to a recent change — a deploy, a config push, a vendor patch, a cert rotation. 'It was working yesterday' tells you to check today's change-log before forming an exotic theory. Recent changes are the highest-priors of the bug space.

flashcards.front: What's the divide-and-conquer technique?
flashcards.back: Bisect the path between symptom and cause. If 10 hops between client and server, test hop 5. Good → problem is past hop 5. Bad → problem is before. Two more bisections narrow it to one hop. Faster than checking every link sequentially when the chain is long.

dockerfile.title: Dockerfiles and image building
dockerfile.intro: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building a container image — a sequence of instructions that produce immutable, layered, portable artifacts. The exam wants you to know which instructions create layers, how the cache works, and how to keep images small and secure.

flashcards.front: Which Dockerfile instructions create a new layer?
flashcards.back: RUN, COPY, ADD each create a new read-only layer in the image. CMD, ENTRYPOINT, ENV, WORKDIR, EXPOSE update image metadata but don't create layers. Layer count affects image size and build cache hit rate.

flashcards.front: Multi-stage builds — what's the point?
flashcards.back: First stage installs build tools (compilers, package managers) and produces an artifact. Second stage copies ONLY the artifact into a minimal runtime image. Final image is tiny (no build deps) and surface-area for vulnerabilities is small. Standard pattern for Go, Java, Node production builds.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
flashcards.back: ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs. CMD provides default arguments (overridable at `docker run` time). The two combine: ENTRYPOINT ["nginx"] + CMD ["-g", "daemon off;"]. Override at runtime: `docker run myimg -h` runs `nginx -h`. Use ENTRYPOINT to lock in 'what this container IS'.

flashcards.front: Why pin base image versions instead of `:latest`?
flashcards.back: `latest` is a moving target — your build is non-reproducible. Today's `python:latest` might be 3.12; next month it's 3.13 and your code breaks subtly. Pin to a specific tag (`python:3.12-slim`) or, for compliance, a digest (`python@sha256:...`). Update intentionally, not by accident.

protocols.title: Network protocols
protocols.intro: Every networking exam tests the same handful of protocols: HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, DHCP, ARP, ICMP, NTP. Knowing what each does, which port it uses, and what a failure looks like solves most question stems.

flashcards.front: DHCP — what's the DORA exchange?
flashcards.back: Client broadcasts DISCOVER ('any DHCP servers there?'). Servers reply OFFER (an IP + lease terms). Client picks one and broadcasts REQUEST. Server replies ACK confirming the lease. Failures: no DORA → check DHCP server, relay agent, or VLAN configuration.

flashcards.front: ARP — what does it resolve?
flashcards.back: IP-to-MAC mapping inside one broadcast domain. To send a packet to `10.0.0.5`, the host first checks its ARP cache; if missing, it broadcasts 'who has 10.0.0.5?' and the target replies with its MAC. ARP is L2-only — once a router forwards the packet, a new ARP happens on the next segment.

flashcards.front: ICMP — what's it actually used for?
flashcards.back: Error reporting (destination unreachable, TTL exceeded, fragmentation needed) and diagnostics (ping = echo request/reply, traceroute = TTL-exceeded responses). Often blocked at firewalls 'because security', which breaks path-MTU discovery — usually a mistake.

flashcards.front: Common port numbers — name HTTP, HTTPS, SSH, DNS, SMTP.
flashcards.back: HTTP: 80. HTTPS: 443. SSH: 22. DNS: 53 (UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers and large responses). SMTP: 25 (server-to-server) or 587 (submission from clients). Memorize the common ones; the rest are searchable.

hardware.title: PC hardware
hardware.intro: CompTIA A+ and similar exams test physical hardware: connectors, motherboard layout, power, storage, RAM types. The trick is matching the symptom to the component — boot failures usually mean RAM/power/CMOS battery, slow disk means thermals or imminent failure.

flashcards.front: DDR3 vs DDR4 vs DDR5 — what changes?
flashcards.back: Each generation roughly doubles peak bandwidth and lowers operating voltage. DDR3 = 1.5V, DDR4 = 1.2V, DDR5 = 1.1V. Slots are keyed differently — you cannot physically install the wrong generation. Mixing speeds in dual-channel makes them run at the slowest speed.

flashcards.front: M.2 NVMe vs M.2 SATA vs 2.5" SATA — which is fastest?
flashcards.back: M.2 NVMe (uses PCIe lanes): 3,500-7,000 MB/s read. M.2 SATA (M.2 form factor but SATA bus): ~550 MB/s. 2.5" SATA: also ~550 MB/s. The same M.2 slot may accept both; the motherboard manual tells you which keys (B-key SATA, M-key NVMe) it supports.

flashcards.front: What does the CMOS battery do?
flashcards.back: Powers the CMOS chip that stores BIOS/UEFI settings and the real-time clock when the system is unplugged. Symptoms of a dead one: clock resets to default on every boot, BIOS settings revert, occasional 'CMOS checksum error'. Coin cell CR2032, $1 fix.

flashcards.front: POST beep codes — what do they mean?
flashcards.back: Power-On Self-Test diagnostic beeps from the motherboard speaker before video init. Single short beep = pass. Repeating short beeps = memory error. Long-short-short = video problem. Each BIOS vendor has a slightly different code chart — check the motherboard manual.

functions.title: Serverless functions
functions.intro: Functions-as-a-Service (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions) execute short-lived code in response to events. No servers, no patching, auto-scaling. The exam tests triggers, integration patterns, and the limits that bite at scale.

flashcards.front: Triggers — what fires a function?
flashcards.back: HTTP request (API Gateway, HTTP trigger), object storage event (file uploaded), queue message (SQS, Service Bus, Pub/Sub), schedule (cron / EventBridge), database stream (DynamoDB Streams, Change Feed). One function, many possible triggers — the runtime hands you the event payload.

flashcards.front: What is the function's execution context?
flashcards.back: The runtime environment that persists between invocations on the same warm instance. Things defined OUTSIDE the handler (DB connections, cached secrets, imported modules) are reused on the next invocation — huge perf win. Anything inside the handler runs every time.

flashcards.front: Idempotency — why does serverless need it?
flashcards.back: Most event sources retry on failure: SQS delivers at-least-once, S3 events can fire twice for a single upload, EventBridge retries on 5xx. Your function MUST tolerate the same event twice (use idempotency keys, conditional writes, dedup tables) or you'll double-charge a customer.

flashcards.front: Concurrency limits — what's the trap?
flashcards.back: AWS Lambda's account-level concurrency cap is 1000 by default. A sudden traffic spike can starve other functions in the account. Mitigations: reserved concurrency (guarantees a slice for a critical function), provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed instances), per-function quotas.

cloud-concepts.title: Cloud fundamentals
cloud-concepts.intro: Every cloud certification starts with the same vocabulary: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS, public / private / hybrid, capex vs opex, elasticity, regions and AZs. Getting these right is half the foundational exam.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — pick an example of each.
flashcards.back: IaaS (Infrastructure): EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine — you manage OS and up. PaaS (Platform): App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk, App Service — you manage code, provider manages runtime. SaaS (Software): Gmail, Salesforce — you just use it. As you go up the stack, you get convenience, lose control.

flashcards.front: Region vs Availability Zone — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic area (us-east-1, europe-west2). An AZ is one or more data centers inside a region with independent power/cooling/network. AZs in a region are connected by low-latency fiber but isolated from each other's failures. Best practice: spread workload across 2-3 AZs for HA.

flashcards.front: Elasticity vs scalability — different things?
flashcards.back: Scalability: the system can be grown (add capacity to handle 10x load). Elasticity: it auto-shrinks back when load drops — you don't pay for idle capacity. A scalable system isn't necessarily elastic (a manually-resized DB is scalable but not elastic). Cloud's killer feature is being both.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud favor opex?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): big upfront purchase (a server, a building). Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing per-unit cost (cloud usage, electricity). Cloud turns infrastructure into opex — no $500k server purchases, just monthly bills. Easier for finance to scale, easier to abandon a project without sunk cost.

identity.title: Identity providers and federation
identity.intro: Modern identity is centralized — one identity provider issues tokens that every application trusts. SAML and OIDC are the two interop standards. Federation means trusting another organization's identity provider for cross-org access.

flashcards.front: SAML vs OIDC — what's the practical difference?
flashcards.back: SAML: XML, browser-redirect-heavy, used for enterprise SSO into web apps. OIDC (on top of OAuth 2.0): JSON, mobile- and SPA-friendly, the modern default. New integrations should use OIDC; existing SAML works fine, no urgent reason to migrate.

flashcards.front: What's an IdP vs an SP (service provider)?
flashcards.back: Identity Provider: where users actually authenticate (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, Auth0). Service Provider: the app the user is trying to use (Slack, Salesforce, your custom app). The IdP issues a signed token; the SP trusts the IdP's signature and reads the user's identity from the token.

flashcards.front: MFA — why is push notification preferred over SMS?
flashcards.back: SMS is sniffable (SS7 attacks) and SIM-swappable. Push (Duo, Microsoft Authenticator, OS-level biometric) is bound to a specific device, requires user interaction, harder to phish. WebAuthn / FIDO2 hardware keys are the gold standard — phishing-resistant by design.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning — what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Instead of pre-creating users in every app, JIT creates the user on first SSO login, hydrated from the IdP's attributes. Onboarding a new hire: add to the IdP group once, every app that supports JIT auto-creates them on first visit. Deprovisioning is the inverse — IdP removes them, apps refuse next login.
